sections: 2.1 Adaptations from the Original Protocol to Our Context
2.2 Corpus Generation and Recording of Usage
evidence:
It’s Like a Dark Patterns Paradise 3

2.1 Adaptations from the Original Protocol to Our Context

With the following adaptations, our work provides an initial classification of DPs
in trending Brazilian apps and a comparison with previous studies from other
countries [3,20].

Corpus Generation. We used nine categories by adding "Tools", compared
to the eight in Di Geronimo’s study. We also reduced our sample to 100 apps,
fewer than Di Geronimo’s 240.

Recording and Classification. We added a test phase to determine our
recording method and find necessary protocol changes. For this, recording and
classification procedures of Di Geronimo’s study [3] were performed for two pairs
of researchers in 9 different apps. One pair used their own Android smartphones,
and the other pair used an emulator. We selected the emulator as the official
method to keep consistency between devices and budget limitations. Testing
shows that DPs were detectable in emulator recordings as well as in smartphone
recordings. Based on this test, we added the “checking the terms of service and
privacy policy” task. This phase helps to consolidate consistency in the analysis
between our two researcher pairs (utilizing a rotation method, different from Di
Geronimo’s single pair) and leads to identifying potential new findings. Apps
used in the test were re-recorded by a different researcher (to avoid bias) and
used in the final analysis.

New Usage Contexts. We added the macro class Linguistic Dead-Ends and
its subclass Untranslation, discovered by Hidaka et al. [20] to our study because
of their presence in the test phase. Furthermore, we identified new findings of
specific contexts of DP not reported by Di Geronimo, resulting in six new cases
of DP described in the results section.

2.2 Corpus Generation and Recording of Usage

To generate a corpus for the study, we first examined the top 100 trending general
apps in the Brazilian Google Play Store [6] on January 19th, 2025. We searched
for the uses of the app, suspicious reviews, and the most frequent categories in
the 100 most popular apps, then we tried to fit those apps in the categories
reported by Di Geronimo (Communication, Entertainment, Family, Music &
Audio, News & Magazines, Photography, Shopping, and Social).
In this initial overview, we noted the presence of the app categories Tools
and Finance, which aren’t within the scope of Di Geronimo [3]. We added them
to our scope since each represents 16% (16 apps) of the top 100 trending apps.
During the recording phase, we discovered that the Finance category doesn’t
work on emulators, so we removed it from the future steps. We used Sensor
Tower for the final selection [19] on January 22nd, 2025, following four criteria:
(i) It must be available to Android devices; (ii) It must be free to download; (iii)
It must be trending in Brazil; (iv) It must be trending in its category.
We did not include apps that were: (i) Not available for download; (ii) Not
available in Brazil; (iii) Included in another category; (iv) “Launcher” Apps; (v)

4 L. Ribeiro et al.

Required a subscription to access its main features; (vi) Tied to the citizen’s ID
and used to access governmental services.
We approved 12 trending apps in each category for the analysis phase. Some
apps malfunctioned in the emulator, resulting in the analysis approval of 100
apps divided into the following structure: 12 in Family; 12 in Music & Audio;
12 in News & Magazines; 12 in Photography; 12 in Social; 11 in Shopping; 11 in
Tools; 9 in Communication; 9 in Entertainment.
We used BlueStacks 5 [1] to emulate the Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra and
run the apps. To capture the screen, we used a native tool on desktops powered
by Windows. Each researcher created a new Gmail account. We also purchased
a SIM card and plugged it into a smartphone to validate its use in apps that
required a phone number. To ensure consistency in the usage, we recorded the
first 10 minutes of the selected apps following eight tasks (when available): (i)
creating an account and log out; (ii) closing and reopening the app; (iii) visiting
the market page; (iv) going to the setting page; (v) checking the terms of service
and privacy policy; (vi) continuing shopping until checkout; (vii) trying to select
product names in e-shopping; (viii) using the app for its intended use. We did
not purchase any products or services in the apps.

2.3 DPs Classification

We organized ourselves into two pairs. While one pair was recording the usage,
the other was analyzing the videos. Once we had already analyzed the first
half of the apps, we switched roles. During the classification process, we first
analyzed the videos individually. Then, we discussed them together to mitigate
DP Blindness. The agreement between the pairs was good according to Weighted
Cohen’s Kappa ( κ = 0.64) which indicates substantial agreement. We included
a third researcher to break ties when the pair did not reach an agreement.
Di Geronimo’s expansion [3] of Gray’s taxonomy [9], together with Hidaka’s
later findings related to linguistic DPs [20], based our classification process.
Therefore, the taxonomy used in this study divides the DPs into six macro
classes: (i) Nagging; (ii) Obstruction including three subclasses (Intermediate
Currency, Price Comparison Prevention, and Roach Motel); (iii) Sneaking in-
cluding four subclasses (Bait and Switch, Hidden Information, Preselection, and
Sneak into Basket); (iv) Interface Interferences including five subclasses (Dis-
guised Ad, Aesthetic Manipulation, Toying with Emotions, False Hierarchy, and
Trick Question); (v) Forced Action including two subclasses (Privacy Zuchering
and Disguised Ad); (vi) Linguistic Dead-End including the subclass Untransla-
tion. Besides the macro class Linguistic Dead-Ends defined by Hidaka [20], the
macro classes and subclasses are defined in detail in Gray’s study [9].
Alongside the types of DPs, we also followed a guide of 40 specific DP
cases [16] to address the subjectivity of identifying DPs based solely on their
descriptions. There were DP cases that fit more directly with the macro class it-
self. For this reason, Nagging, Obstruction, and Forced Action are macro classes
that also function as unique subclasses within themselves. Additionally, to en-

8 L. Ribeiro et al.

The comparison of our findings with those of Di Geronimo and Hidaka reveals
differences in the expression of DPs in each context (e.g., the DP occurrence sur-
plus in 10 out of 16 subclasses, compared with Hidaka’s findings). This suggests
that various socioeconomic, educational, and sociocultural factors may influence
how, where, and when DPs are manifested. Future research conducted in vari-
ous contexts should expand this discussion and provide new insights into how
cultural differences influence the presence of DPs.

5 Limitations

Our scope contains trending free apps on the Brazilian Google Play Store. We
recorded 10 minutes of the first use of each app; any deviation from this prede-
termined scope may generate new and different results. Moreover, some interac-
tions—and consequently DPs—might be limited or vary in an extended usage
scenario. Despite the sample reduction, we found similar results, indicating that
the impact was not substantial.
The intention behind using the emulator was to replicate the experience of a
real smartphone. However, a specific subset of DPs may not appear in emulated
applications. In certain instances, specific apps were inaccessible because they
flagged the emulator as suspicious for usage.

6 Conclusion

After analyzing 100 trending mobile apps in Brazil, we found an average of 7.51
DPs/app and six new cases of use of known dark patterns in the Brazilian con-
text. The results showed key differences compared to contexts in the United
States [3] and Japan [20] (e.g., average DPs per app, common DP subclass).
Our findings enhance the understanding of DPs and their consequences in soci-
eties beyond the WEIRD classification, promoting a more comprehensive view
of the topic, especially within Brazilian culture. Future work should explore the
presence of DPs in Finance apps and expand research by using a larger corpus
that considers more representatives of the Global South and their unique as-
pects as non-WEIRD societies. We encourage the HCI community to broaden
its perspective and actively research how DPs affect society’s economy, popula-
tion well-being, and culture beyond the WEIRD spectrum.

7 Acknowledgments

This paper is a partial result of the project “Digital Well-Being” , supported
by the Brazilian agency National Council for Scientific and Technological De-
velopment (CNPq/MCTI, Call No. 10/2023 – Universal), under grant number
404559/2023-9, coordinated by Dr. Ticianne Darin.

V. Safety by Design Principles

While four over-arching principles were initially

developed, two of the principles were combined

following feedback received during consultations.

As a result, three over-arching high-level principles

were drafted to provide clear guidance to industry

to help them develop services that harness the

benefits and potential of the online world, while

mitigating against real risks and harms.

The principles set out the measures that eSafety

encourages and envisages online and digital

services will take to ensure that the safety of

users is suitably addressed and considered during

the design, development and deployment of their

service. While voluntary, adopting the principles will

set industries apart in the marketplace, allowing

companies to show global leadership in developing

responsible, value and safety-centred online

products and services.

Good practice notes have also been provided

as part of the Principles to guide industry in

understanding and implementing the principles

and highlighting that the principles are achievable,

realistic and actionable. These were highlighted

during the consultation process as effective,

although there is no robust evidence about the

effectiveness and impact of these practices. As

such, the good practice notes should be viewed as

illustrations only, and act as a guide.

The principles that sit underneath each overarching

high-level principle have been ranked according

to the sense of urgency with which they need to

be addressed — a point which was highlighted by

all three stakeholder groups in consultation. While

services are encouraged to address each principle,

greater attention and focus should be placed on

meeting the higher ranked principles.

Safety by Design 25

Good practice note ( Principle 1.6)

LEGO has developed a risk assessment tool

against which every new feature and architectural

component is weighed. The legal and child safety

teams provide developers

with sets of measures and stop-gaps which the

development team then assess and address

before a product or feature can be brought to

market.

Facebook has developed an internal functional

expert review through which all products

have to pass. These reviews involve experts in

privacy, safety and security from both within the

organisation and external to it
75
.

Cybersecurity company Two Hat Security has

produced briefing documents that outline

workflows for moderating different types of

content for online services.

Crisp, a language analysis firm, has developed

AI to profile both users and online spaces, so

that moderation attention can focus on areas of

the service which attract those with nefarious

intentions or where interactions are taking a

negative turn. This profiling information allows

services to assess existing features or to make

the necessary changes to the online environment

to curb this activity.

Principle 1.6: Prepare documented risk management

and impact assessments to assess and remediate

any potential safety harms that could be enabled or

facilitated by the product or service

Determining community standards (Principle 1.2) is

vital for developing robust, efficient and evidenced

workflows that will effectively moderate and

remediate safety risks and harms on services. The

risks and harms experienced by users are well

catalogued, with three main themes of risk and

five overarching categories of harm identified (see

page 3). As such, services can use these to develop

both the boundaries of acceptable behaviour

and the level of risk acceptance for the service
74
.

This process enables services to determine what

functions it will offer users, what methods of

moderation and escalation will be developed, and

the restrictions that will be put in place to avert

known risks.

Moderation workflows will develop and evolve over

time, as the service gains popularity or is used in

specific ways by the user community. The more

data and information that the service has about

how its service is being used and abused, the

easier it is for the service to adapt workflows to

prioritise and target risks. A host of outsourcing

options are available for services that do not have

the internal capacity to manage content moderation

themselves.

Risk thresholds can be developed for both content

and conduct, with users subject to different levels

of oversight depending on their risk profile, or how

new they are to the service. For example, new

users, and users who are repeatedly disruptive or

post content outside the acceptable thresholds for

the service, can be subjected to higher levels of

assessment from the service.

Services that target young users (under the age of

12) tend to be much more risk averse than those

which target adult populations. As such,

pre-moderation is often a prerequisite to uploading

any content to services catering for children.

Notwithstanding measures taken on age-specific

sites, research shows that children can and

frequently do access material on services that are

age-inappropriate. This behoves all services to

consider adopting measures equivalent to those

employed by child-focused services.

As risk profiles can change over time, the service

provider or technology vendor may need to perform

risk audits to ensure that they are continuing to

exercise good practice when it comes to addressing

safety risks.

74 See Two Hat Security paper on ‘How to Moderate Images Efficiently: Save Time, Money, and Resources with these Sample Workflows’.

75 Please see www.facebook.com/notes/facebook-australia-policy/how-can-facebook-do-more-to-reduce-bullying/2178124645848130/

question: Por que a prevalência de padrões no Interact não substitui as métricas de eficácia e responsabilização discutidas no princípio 3.4 de Safety by Design?
answer: O Interact descreve [[presença, distribuição e quantidade de casos]] em cem apps; não acompanha a redução de dano após uma política ou moderação. SbD 3.4 propõe publicação de análises significativas sobre abusos, esforços de moderação e cumprimento das regras, distinguindo escala de denúncias da avaliação de eficácia. A correlação ajuda a separar uma linha de base descritiva da pergunta sobre [[o que uma medida preventiva realmente muda]]. Nem a prevalência observada prova falha causal de uma prática específica, nem a publicação de um relatório prova proteção. As notas SbD são ilustrativas, e os dois documentos exigem cuidado para que números de atividade não sejam tratados automaticamente como resultados de bem-estar.

While four over-arching principles were initially

developed, two of the principles were combined

following feedback received during consultations.

were drafted to provide clear guidance to industry

to help them develop services that harness the

benefits and potential of the online world, while

mitigating against real risks and harms.

The principles set out the measures that eSafety

encourages and envisages online and digital

services will take to ensure that the safety of

users is suitably addressed and considered during

the design, development and deployment of their

service. While voluntary, adopting the principles will

set industries apart in the marketplace, allowing

companies to show global leadership in developing

responsible, value and safety-centred online

products and services.

Good practice notes have also been provided

as part of the Principles to guide industry in

understanding and implementing the principles

and highlighting that the principles are achievable,

realistic and actionable. These were highlighted

during the consultation process as effective,

although there is no robust evidence about the

effectiveness and impact of these practices. As

such, the good practice notes should be viewed as

illustrations only, and act as a guide.

The principles that sit underneath each overarching

high-level principle have been ranked according

to the sense of urgency with which they need to

be addressed — a point which was highlighted by

all three stakeholder groups in consultation. While

services are encouraged to address each principle,

greater attention and focus should be placed on

meeting the higher ranked principles.

eSafety Commissioner 34

Principle 3.5: Commit to innovating and investing

in safety-enhancing technology, as well as

collaborating and sharing safety-enhancing tools,

best practices and technology

Advancements in technology, machine-learning and

artificial intelligence have the potential to radically

transform user safety and online experiences.

In order to harness and promote innovation and

investment in user safety, a commitment among

and within services to collaborating and pushing

the boundaries on addressing and combatting

online harms should expedite the development of a

new wave of safety-enhancing technology.

Good practice note ( Principle 3.4)

Facebook, Google and Twitter have all published

transparency reports in the last 12 months in

a commitment to a more open exchange of

information.

Facebook released its first Community Standards

Enforcement report in May 2018, and which

was updated in November 2018 to cover eight

categories of violations. Facebook have identified

five measurement metrics that will be used in

future reports, with two metrics still being under

development. The five community standards

enforcement measures are: prevalence of

community standards violations, quantity of

content actioned, quantity of content actioned by

detection technology and trained teams before

items are flagged by users, speed of action

based on impact of violating content (under

development), and accuracy of actions based on

reviews (under development).

Twitter released its 13th biannual transparency

report late in 2018, which included a new section

‘Twitter Rules enforcement’ that provides data

and insights into the enforcement of abuse,

hateful conduct, private information, child

sexual exploitation, sensitive media and violent

threats. Twitter have committed to evolving

their approach to transparency to ensure it is

comprehensive, clear, contextual and meaningful.

The Internet Commission
83
, based in the UK,

is currently in the process of developing an

independent transparency reporting framework,

as part of its dialogue on digital responsibility. The

transparency framework identifies key indicators

to better uncover the impact and effectiveness

of content moderation processes and practices

within services.

New America recently published ‘The

Transparency Reporting Toolkit: Content

Takedown Reporting
84
, which identifies best

practice for content reporting takedowns

across six categories — including Community

Guidelines-based content takedowns.

question: Como o caso de termos em outro idioma se relaciona ao §12 do Art. 48 local, preservando o alcance específico da disposição?
answer: O Interact descreve termos ou política de privacidade em outro idioma, apesar de o app estar no idioma do usuário, como barreira informacional. No documento local do Art. 48, o §12 se refere aos [[termos de uso dos fornecedores de serviços digitais que hospedem conteúdo de terceiros]] e à informação clara e acessível sobre a indicação etária atribuída pelo órgão competente ou, na ausência, pelo modelo autorizado. A comparação permite discutir como a barreira de idioma pode tensionar acesso à informação. Não transforma o §12 em exigência genérica de traduzir qualquer documento de todo aplicativo, nem prova infração jurídica de um app analisado. Não se verifica vigência normativa aqui.

We did not find any statistically significant difference in any app category. Di
Geronimo and Hidaka also failed the test and did not find any correlations
between the number of DPs and the app categories. This test supports the
hypothesis of the pervasive nature of DPs. A Kruskal-Wallis test ( χ
2 
= 520, p
< .001) revealed a significant difference between the DP subclasses. A Dwass-
Steel-Critchlow-Fligner pairwise comparisons showed that the Nagging subclass
is significantly higher than all other subclasses, except when comparing to Forced
Action (W = -5.6466, p = 0.008).
Our findings also revealed six DP cases previously unreported in international
research. They demonstrate novel applications of known DPs: (i) “ Terms/Policy
in Another Language ” (Untranslation case) when crucial information for the
user (terms of service or privacy policy) is in another language, even if the app
is in the native user language, creating a barrier between the user and the in-
formation; (ii) “ Terms/Policy Out of Bounds ” (Obstruction case) redirects
the user to an external page, typically a web page, to access the terms of service
or privacy policy, increasing unnecessary stress and reducing the likelihood of
reading; (iii) “ Ads with layers ” (Obstruction case) specifies chains of multiple
time-delayed sub-ads to extend user exposure within the same content, making
more than one “attention call” in the same time span; (iv) “ Task-based Re-
wards ” (Forced Action case) describes cases where the app presents a mission
beyond the main flow, that when completed rewards the user with some aspect
of the app services; (v) “ Ad-locked Rewards ” (Forced Action case) indicates
when the user is forced to watch an advertisement to receive a reward like vir-
tual coins, time accelerators, or other bonuses; (vi) “ Evoke Emotions to Take
Action ” (Toying with Emotions case) specifies uses of any language or other
appealing visual elements to persuade the user into an action. Those DP cases
occur 158 times in our classification, accounting for approximately 21% of the
751 DPs found presenting specific occurrences of: Terms/Policy in Another Lan-
guage (45 times); Terms/Policy Out of Bounds (26 times); Ads with Layers (42

It’s Like a Dark Patterns Paradise 7

times); Task-based Rewards (20 times); Ad-locked Rewards (14 times); Evoke
Emotions to Take Action (11 times).
Real-world examples of each of the new DP cases are available in the study’s
database on Zenodo [16].

4 Discussions

The discovery of six new cases of dark patterns, which constitute approximately
21% of the reported DPs, provides a more specific and consistent classification
of these patterns. This new classification aligns the previous list of DP cases
more closely with the Brazilian context. Additionally, it suggests that apps in
Brazil (whether local or international) are employing innovative strategies to
discourage usage and prompt users to take action, beyond merely displaying ads
or pop-ups. These strategies often involve creating new tasks that engage users
in activities beneficial to the developer, such as enabling notifications for app
updates or using persuasive messages to encourage users to rate the app.
Our results indicate that the presence of DPs in Brazilian apps aligns closely
with those in American apps, with an average score of 7.51 compared to Di
Geronimo’s 7.4, and a prevalence of 96% versus Di Geronimo’s 95%. However,
the distribution of these results in the DP subclasses differentiates these two
scenarios. When analyzing the most recurring subclasses, it is interesting to
note that even though Nagging is in first place in both surveys, Brazilian apps
stand out in the percentage difference (34,5%).
A broader perspective on this distribution difference reveals that in Brazil,
apps often use DPs that aim to manipulate users by directing them to alternative
activities, while in the US, they tend to manipulate users by tricking them into
making specific decisions and taking certain actions. The three most common
DPs tried to obstruct or force the user to interact with the application. Therefore,
there is an increase in the number of cases involving Nagging and Forced Action
in the Brazilian context. Moreover, the fourth most common is Untranslation
(Linguistic Dead-Ends), appearing at least once in 45% of the apps.
However, when comparing our results with Hidaka’s findings [20], we found
an increase in presence per app on 10 out of the 16 subclasses considered in the
analyses. This suggests that the Japanese DP situation appears to be handled
more strictly compared to the Brazilian one. This could be due to cultural, le-
gal, and market differences. Further, the subclasses with the most increase were
Aesthetic Manipulation (171,40%), Unstranslation (100%) and Trick Question
(100%). The most decrease being Hidden Information (-116,60%), Roach Motal
(-100%), and Intermediate Currency (-60%). Furthermore, the substantial in-
crease in the Unstranslation subclass in the Brazilian context draws attention
to a misuse of language that intentionally obscures information by utilizing a
foreign language, even when the rest of the app is in the user’s native language.
Those differences, particularly the Untranslation, should be addressed in future
works about DPs in Brazil, since the population has a score considered low in
proficiency tests such as the EF English Proficiency Index [4].

question: Ao correlacionar Ads with Layers e Ad-locked Rewards com funcionalidades do §10 do Art. 48, por que é preciso distinguir mecanismo de interface de critério classificatório?
answer: No Interact, Ads with Layers prolonga exposição por cadeias de subanúncios e Ad-locked Rewards condiciona benefícios à visualização publicitária. O Art. 48 local considera funcionalidades e conteúdos na atribuição da classificação, incluindo interação que favoreça compulsividade e exemplos de [[manutenção do usuário ativo por períodos prolongados]], como recompensas variáveis, notificações e gamificação. A ponte é analítica: mecanismos concretos ajudam a formular perguntas sobre condições de uso. Não significa que toda publicidade, recompensa ou gamificação seja um dark pattern, nem que um critério classificatório meça o dano causado por ele. O estudo de apps tampouco demonstra a eficácia ou a aplicação jurídica da classificação.

question: Como as barreiras observadas em políticas e termos podem dialogar com controles parentais e moderação considerados pelo Art. 48, sem equiparar classificação a segurança?
answer: O Interact identifica fricções de acesso e compreensão em informações relevantes ao usuário. O documento local do Art. 48, nos §§14–15, considera [[controle editorial e curadoria, ferramentas de controle etário e parental acessíveis e políticas de moderação]], remetendo especificações aos Guias Práticos. A correlação permite discutir que um recurso listado precisa ser analisado no contexto em que a pessoa o encontra e compreende, e que a classificação envolve fatores além de um rótulo. Contudo, o Interact não testou a eficácia desses controles, e os parágrafos não demonstram que classificar um serviço elimina os padrões observados. Os Guias não fornecidos não podem ser preenchidos com conhecimento externo; não se afirma vigência do documento.

The comparison of our findings with those of Di Geronimo and Hidaka reveals
differences in the expression of DPs in each context (e.g., the DP occurrence sur-
plus in 10 out of 16 subclasses, compared with Hidaka’s findings). This suggests
that various socioeconomic, educational, and sociocultural factors may influence
how, where, and when DPs are manifested. Future research conducted in vari-
ous contexts should expand this discussion and provide new insights into how
cultural differences influence the presence of DPs.

5 Limitations

Our scope contains trending free apps on the Brazilian Google Play Store. We
recorded 10 minutes of the first use of each app; any deviation from this prede-
termined scope may generate new and different results. Moreover, some interac-
tions—and consequently DPs—might be limited or vary in an extended usage
scenario. Despite the sample reduction, we found similar results, indicating that
the impact was not substantial.
The intention behind using the emulator was to replicate the experience of a
real smartphone. However, a specific subset of DPs may not appear in emulated
applications. In certain instances, specific apps were inaccessible because they
flagged the emulator as suspicious for usage.

6 Conclusion

After analyzing 100 trending mobile apps in Brazil, we found an average of 7.51
DPs/app and six new cases of use of known dark patterns in the Brazilian con-
text. The results showed key differences compared to contexts in the United
States [3] and Japan [20] (e.g., average DPs per app, common DP subclass).
Our findings enhance the understanding of DPs and their consequences in soci-
eties beyond the WEIRD classification, promoting a more comprehensive view
of the topic, especially within Brazilian culture. Future work should explore the
presence of DPs in Finance apps and expand research by using a larger corpus
that considers more representatives of the Global South and their unique as-
pects as non-WEIRD societies. We encourage the HCI community to broaden
its perspective and actively research how DPs affect society’s economy, popula-
tion well-being, and culture beyond the WEIRD spectrum.

question: Como a barreira linguística de Untranslation e o creator-consumer divide podem ser articulados sem reduzir a vulnerabilidade a uma incapacidade individual?
answer: O Interact observa [[informação crucial em idioma estrangeiro]] e discute desigualdades educacionais, letramento digital e acesso tecnológico como parte de um contexto heterogêneo. CHIP propõe o creator-consumer divide como lente para assimetrias estruturais entre onde jogos são criados e onde são consumidos, incluindo precariedade e exportação de perspectivas WEIRD. A síntese desloca a pergunta de uma suposta falha individual para [[condições de design, compreensão e poder]]. Isso não prova que o divide causou cada caso de Untranslation, nem transfere a prevalência dos cem apps para jogos ou todo o Sul Global. O argumento de CHIP é teórico e especulativo; o Interact oferece um diagnóstico observacional delimitado.

Further, determining whether the Brazilian context is WEIRD or non-WEIRD
is difficult, due to its complex social indicators [11]. The complexity of this sit-
uation creates new challenges for the HCI community. Thus, it presents a criti-
cal context for investigation of DPs impact, representing a large digital market
within the Global South with specific characteristics in questions such as inequal-
ity in education [5], lack of digital literacy [21] and uneven spread of Information
and Communication Technologies (ICTs) [10], because of that we hypothesize
that DPs in Brazilian context have particularities.
Inspired by the culture-specific DPs found in Japan, which are linked to lin-
guistic characteristics [20], this work explores context-specific aspects in Brazil
regarding DPs. We aim to present baseline data on the Brazilian prevalence
and types of DPs, establishing a point of comparison with results from research
studies in the United States [3] and Japan [20]. Specifically, we investigate (i)
the frequency and types of DPs in the most widely used Brazilian apps, catego-
rized according to established classifications; (ii) how they contrast with previous
research conducted in other geographical settings.
To this end, we adapted the qualitative expert classification protocol of Di
Geronimo et al. [3] and included the DP class introduced by Hidaka et al. [20].
We analyzed the top 100 trending

Android apps in Brazil across 9 categories,
classifying identified DPs based on a taxonomy derived from Gray et al. [9],
Di Geronimo et al. [3], Hidaka et al. [20] and additions we made to it: 6 new
DP cases found in the Brazilian context. Our work contributions include: (i)
Identifying a baseline DP prevalence in popular Brazilian mobile apps (96%
affected, averaging 7.51 DPs/app).; (ii) Identifying higher rates of Nagging and
Forced Action in Brazil compared to results from United States [3] and Japan
[20]; (iii) Presenting and discussing the prevalent DPs in Brazil and the notable
presence (45% of apps) of Untranslation, offering context-specific insights for
future Global South research on DPs.

2 Methodology

We replicate the methodology of Di Geronimo et al. [3] with a focus on the
Brazilian context to identify differences and similarities in the presence and
frequency of DPs in the Brazilian apps. However, we adjusted the procedure of
the original study to address limitations and incorporate emerging findings from
our own study. The resultant database is available on Zenodo [16].

ratings, reviews, and downloads.

We did not find any statistically significant difference in any app category. Di
Geronimo and Hidaka also failed the test and did not find any correlations
between the number of DPs and the app categories. This test supports the
hypothesis of the pervasive nature of DPs. A Kruskal-Wallis test ( χ

is significantly higher than all other subclasses, except when comparing to Forced
Action (W = -5.6466, p = 0.008).
Our findings also revealed six DP cases previously unreported in international
research. They demonstrate novel applications of known DPs: (i) “ Terms/Policy
in Another Language ” (Untranslation case) when crucial information for the
user (terms of service or privacy policy) is in another language, even if the app
is in the native user language, creating a barrier between the user and the in-
formation; (ii) “ Terms/Policy Out of Bounds ” (Obstruction case) redirects
the user to an external page, typically a web page, to access the terms of service
or privacy policy, increasing unnecessary stress and reducing the likelihood of
reading; (iii) “ Ads with layers ” (Obstruction case) specifies chains of multiple
time-delayed sub-ads to extend user exposure within the same content, making
more than one “attention call” in the same time span; (iv) “ Task-based Re-
wards ” (Forced Action case) describes cases where the app presents a mission
beyond the main flow, that when completed rewards the user with some aspect
of the app services; (v) “ Ad-locked Rewards ” (Forced Action case) indicates
when the user is forced to watch an advertisement to receive a reward like vir-
tual coins, time accelerators, or other bonuses; (vi) “ Evoke Emotions to Take
Action ” (Toying with Emotions case) specifies uses of any language or other
appealing visual elements to persuade the user into an action. Those DP cases
occur 158 times in our classification, accounting for approximately 21% of the
751 DPs found presenting specific occurrences of: Terms/Policy in Another Lan-
guage (45 times); Terms/Policy Out of Bounds (26 times); Ads with Layers (42

The comparison of our findings with those of Di Geronimo and Hidaka reveals
differences in the expression of DPs in each context (e.g., the DP occurrence sur-
plus in 10 out of 16 subclasses, compared with Hidaka’s findings). This suggests
that various socioeconomic, educational, and sociocultural factors may influence
how, where, and when DPs are manifested. Future research conducted in vari-
ous contexts should expand this discussion and provide new insights into how
cultural differences influence the presence of DPs.

5 Limitations

Our scope contains trending free apps on the Brazilian Google Play Store. We
recorded 10 minutes of the first use of each app; any deviation from this prede-
termined scope may generate new and different results. Moreover, some interac-
tions—and consequently DPs—might be limited or vary in an extended usage
scenario. Despite the sample reduction, we found similar results, indicating that
the impact was not substantial.
The intention behind using the emulator was to replicate the experience of a
real smartphone. However, a specific subset of DPs may not appear in emulated
applications. In certain instances, specific apps were inaccessible because they
flagged the emulator as suspicious for usage.

6 Conclusion

After analyzing 100 trending mobile apps in Brazil, we found an average of 7.51
DPs/app and six new cases of use of known dark patterns in the Brazilian con-
text. The results showed key differences compared to contexts in the United
States [3] and Japan [20] (e.g., average DPs per app, common DP subclass).
Our findings enhance the understanding of DPs and their consequences in soci-
eties beyond the WEIRD classification, promoting a more comprehensive view
of the topic, especially within Brazilian culture. Future work should explore the
presence of DPs in Finance apps and expand research by using a larger corpus
that considers more representatives of the Global South and their unique as-
pects as non-WEIRD societies. We encourage the HCI community to broaden
its perspective and actively research how DPs affect society’s economy, popula-
tion well-being, and culture beyond the WEIRD spectrum.

Games Made Elsewhere, Harms Felt Here: A Speculative
Perspective of Deceptive Design Impact from the Global South

Ticianne Darin

ticianne@virtual.ufc.br
Federal University of Ceará
Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil

Abstract

This paper uses a speculative design scenario to critique the unequal
power dynamics in global games. It argues that Deceptive Patterns
may function as tools of exploitation, not just manipulation, when
applied to players in the Global South. The work introduces the
creator-consumer divide and calls for equitable collaborations to
confront this emerging form of digital harm.

CCS Concepts

• Human-centered computing → HCI theory, concepts and
models ; • Social and professional topics → Geographic char-
acteristics ; Privacy policies ; • General and reference → Reference
works.

Keywords

Human-Computer Interaction, Video Games, Creator-Consumer Di-
vide, Deceptive Patterns, Dark Patterns, Global South, Speculative
Design, Decoloniality, Regulatory Arbitrage, Predatory Monetiza-
tion, Systemic Vulnerability, WEIRD

ACM Reference Format:

Ticianne Darin. 2025. Games Made Elsewhere, Harms Felt Here: A Specu-
lative Perspective of Deceptive Design Impact from the Global South. In

Companion Proceedings Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction
in Play (CHI PLAY Companion ’25), October 13–16, 2025, Pittsburgh, PA, USA.

ACM, New York, NY, USA, 5 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3744736.3749329

1 Introduction

As a researcher from Brazil, and part of the diverse and complex
makeup often referred to as the "Global South," I continually reflect
on how global research results correspond to our local realities.
Especially in games. Brazil is Latin America’s largest games market
(103 million players [33]). Yet, our global contribution to game
development and research is inconsistent with that data. Brazil
has a very active Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) community,
with a 24-edition national symposium (IHC) and recent Grand
Challenges [25] tailored to our reality. However, there are minimal
funding opportunities for games and play research from the HCI
perspective, as other national priorities take precedence, and a
young, small-scale, and export-oriented domestic game industry [4].

This positions us, like many other non-high-income countries (e.g.,
India, where global publishers often run only support operations
[5]), primarily consumers of games made elsewhere .
The most popular mobile games in Brazil (and India!), e.g., Free
Fire , Roblox , Candy Crush Saga [1, 2] are not only from overseas,
but filled with Deceptive Patterns (DPs) [30]. DPs, formerly known
as Dark Patterns [6], are manipulative designs exploiting user bi-
ases for commercial gain at the user’s expense. In games, they are
intensified by the industry’s shift to "predatory monetization," ob-
scuring true costs [27]. They can cause several harms [7, 23, 24],
and potentially worsen Gaming Disorder (GD) [32, 37]. Yes, games
are also full of DPs in W estern, E ducated, I ndustrialized, R ich, and

D emocratic (WEIRD) contexts. Digital exploitation is not geograph-
ically exclusive. The central question is therefore not if harm occurs
elsewhere, but: Do the vast differences in non-WEIRD contexts alter
the nature and magnitude of that harm? While players in WEIRD
countries, where most of these games are developed, face risks, this
paper argues that the harm can be systemically amplified in major
Global South markets.

2 The Creator-Consumer Divide as a Lens for
Understanding Systemic Player Vulnerability

This paper proposes the creator-consumer divide as a theoretical
construct: a structural schism between creation and consumption
contexts, where vulnerabilities are systemic, pre-existing, and capi-
talized upon via deliberate targeting or indifferent automation. The
divide has two nuances.
First, games as entertainment can lower players’ critical guard
[36], making them more susceptible to manipulative designs dis-
guised as ’part of the game.’ This effect is amplified when a signifi-
cant portion of the population lacks fundamental cognitive defenses,
a vulnerability stemming from deep-seated societal issues in the
Global South. The contrast between the United States (US) and
Brazil illustrates this asymmetry. The US poverty rate is 11.1% [31],
while in Brazil it is over double at 27.4% [14], indicating a more
widespread precarity, which is linked to stress-impaired decision-
making [16]. A paradox of high digital penetration (86.2% [8]) co-
existing with low functional literacy amplifies the situation. While
the US grapples with a substantial illiteracy rate affecting 18% of
its adults, a challenge concentrated mainly in specific minority
and low-income groups [26], Brazil’s issue is more pervasive. 29%
of Brazilians are functionally illiterate (stagnant since 2018), with
another 36% possessing only elementary literacy skills [19, 20]. It
suggests that over half the population may struggle with the criti-
cal thinking skills [34] necessary to defend against manipulative
practices and discourses. This national-scale vulnerability is dis-
tinct from the challenges within specific US communities. Cultural

CHI PLAY Companion ’25, October 13–16, 2025, Pittsburgh, PA, USA Darin, T.

particularities, such as authority norms, can compound these vul-
nerabilities, creating additional exploitation vectors that are also
likely distinct from the creator’s context.
Second, the power imbalance operates structurally through reg-
ulatory arbitrage, exploiting political contexts that, often due to
economic pressures, lack strong and enforceable consumer pro-
tection. Less stringent consumer protection frameworks in many
Global South markets permit the deployment of systems and mon-
etization models that would face greater scrutiny or be prohibited
in other regions, such as the European Union (EU), where coopera-
tion networks work to enhance consumer protection when playing
video games. For instance, while EU principles demand transparent
pricing and respect for consumer vulnerabilities in online gam-
ing [35], their absence in Brazil, as well as in other countries in
the Global South, means that models can systematically obscure
true costs, deny consumers the withdrawal right, and intention-
ally target the most vulnerable players without facing similar legal
repercussions.
So, to what extent does our current game and DP knowledge
apply to non-WEIRD contexts, as research in this topic originates
predominantly from WEIRD contexts [18] (e.g., [11, 13, 15, 22, 29])?
This bias, mirrored in psychology (where WEIRD populations are
12% globally but dominate studies [17]) and broad HCI research
[21], limits findings’ external validity for the global majority and
overlooks socio-economic nuances. From a decolonial perspective
[3, 10], the WEIRD-centricity is not merely a methodological over-
sight; it is a systemic issue. Still, it reflects a more profound power
imbalance, where WEIRD perspectives, values, and designs, includ-
ing those that embed DPs and predatory monetization, are often
uncritically exported and imposed upon diverse global audiences.
Novel DP cases in widely used apps in Brazil [9, 28], most of which
were developed elsewhere, suggest that the context may enable
new forms of exploitation. Is it purposeful or coincidental? Does it
matter?
The creator-consumer divide can serve as a lens to examine
both the impact of manipulative and exploitative game designs
and monetization models on Global South markets, as well as the
potential for a design considered safe in a WEIRD context to become
harmful when deployed in a non-WEIRD one.

3 A Speculative Perspective: Helena and The
Gilded Cage of Ouroboros Seed

This paper uses a speculative design extrapolation [12] to propose
a critical future artifact and an imagined scenario that asks: What
if the creator-consumer divide ensnares individuals in a cycle
where virtual escape consumes real-world essentials and erodes
civic integrity?

Imagine Helena, an archetype of the systemic vulnerability pre-
viously described. Overwhelmed by the precarity of her life, she
turns to her smartphone not just for distraction, but for the sense
of control and achievement her reality denies her. She discovers
Ouroboros Seed. Unlike the simple games she’s used to, it is a
polished title from a huge WEIRD-country-based studio, its ads
promising a vibrant world of community and growth. She doesn’t
know that its state-of-the-art AI engine was prohibited in its home
country for the invasive data extraction used to fuel in-game loops,
nor that it was deployed in Brazil through regulatory arbitrage.
Initially, the game delivers. Its AI-optimized loops provide a
comforting sense of progress, fostering a deep engagement that
soon becomes dependency. The system then creates personalized
crises that make progress dependent on either intense Grinding
[38] or a $18 Pay-to-Skip offer. For Helena, $18 is not disposable
income; it represents the portion of her monthly income for cooking
gas. Her inability to pay is her only defense. But at an AI-calculated
moment of peak desperation, the game presents a different kind
of offer: the ’Community Solidarity Pledge.’ It is not a demand
for immediate cash, but a subtle prompt to pledge a portion of
her upcoming government benefit, the Bolsa Família. Framed as
a pro-social commitment, not a purchase, and designed to exploit
the human bias for immediate relief over a future cost, the offer
bypasses her financial barrier. She sacrifices a piece of her real-
world safety net for a fleeting sense of success in her gilded cage.
But the exploitation does not end with her finances. The rich
psychological profile the AI built on Helena, identifying her anxi-
eties and moments of low cognitive resistance, is sold to political
campaigns for targeted disinformation during a contentious local
election, leveraging the same vulnerabilities the game monetized.

Artifact from the future : The Adaptive Engagement & Resource
Pathway Report for Ouroboros Seed’s developers (Annex A). The
dashboard dehumanizes Helena, reducing her to a set of quantified
vulnerabilities, such as being 92% Prone to ’reactive choices’ in
a ’Scarcity Context.’ It logs triggers designed to weaponize psy-
chological states like ’Scarcity + Anxiety’ and details the harm as
a ’Projected Redistribution’ of resources from her specific urban
district. The corporate euphemism calls a monetization push the
’Harvest Equinox’ seasonal event, and classifies manipulative tactics
as ’Narrative Anchors.’ A final note confirms her profile matches
a ’Civic Tier 2 pattern’ and is flagged for a third-party messaging
test cycle, pending a performative internal ethics review.

Critical Questions: How must HCI’s definition of ’harm’ in
games evolve when designs prey not on universal biases, but on
widespread, structural vulnerabilities? What are our distinct ethical
duties when games are deployed not into isolated pockets of vul-
nerability, but into entire markets where these conditions are the
norm? And when this results in a massive, unidirectional extraction
of value from the Global South, regardless of intent, is it not our
responsibility to name it for what it is: a new form of cognitive
colonialism?
Ouroboro’s speculative dystopia is a provocation. It aims to
make palpable the extreme and deeply inequitable harms that can
arise when the creator-consumer divide in gaming is pushed to its
potential extreme.

4 Toward a Decolonial Game and Play Research

Rooted in my perspective as a researcher from Brazil, this paper
used a speculative scenario to argue that the impact of deceptive
design in games (and potentially other apps) is not uniform. The
proposed theoretical construct, called the creator-consumer divide,
illustrates how the most insidious harm occurs when sophisticated
design exploits pre-existing, systemic vulnerabilities, preying on
the educational deficits, economic precarity, and regulatory gaps

CHIP utiliza [[um cenário especulativo]] no qual Helena enfrenta ciclos de exploração financeira, criação de perfis e consequências cívicas. A comparação é útil para tornar visível a diferença entre documentar uma ocorrência e formular uma hipótese sobre sua trajetória sistêmica. Não há base para dizer que os apps auditados produziram os acontecimentos da ficção, ou que a contagem de padrões mede esses efeitos. A articulação sugere perguntas para investigações futuras de duração e contexto, preservando a distinção entre observação e provocação teórica.

and used to access governmental services.
We approved 12 trending apps in each category for the analysis phase. Some
apps malfunctioned in the emulator, resulting in the analysis approval of 100
apps divided into the following structure: 12 in Family; 12 in Music & Audio;
12 in News & Magazines; 12 in Photography; 12 in Social; 11 in Shopping; 11 in
Tools; 9 in Communication; 9 in Entertainment.
We used BlueStacks 5 [1] to emulate the Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra and
run the apps. To capture the screen, we used a native tool on desktops powered
by Windows. Each researcher created a new Gmail account. We also purchased
a SIM card and plugged it into a smartphone to validate its use in apps that
required a phone number. To ensure consistency in the usage, we recorded the
first 10 minutes of the selected apps following eight tasks (when available): (i)
creating an account and log out; (ii) closing and reopening the app; (iii) visiting
the market page; (iv) going to the setting page; (v) checking the terms of service
and privacy policy; (vi) continuing shopping until checkout; (vii) trying to select
product names in e-shopping; (viii) using the app for its intended use. We did
not purchase any products or services in the apps.

2.3 DPs Classification

We organized ourselves into two pairs. While one pair was recording the usage,
the other was analyzing the videos. Once we had already analyzed the first
half of the apps, we switched roles. During the classification process, we first
analyzed the videos individually. Then, we discussed them together to mitigate
DP Blindness. The agreement between the pairs was good according to Weighted
Cohen’s Kappa ( κ = 0.64) which indicates substantial agreement. We included
a third researcher to break ties when the pair did not reach an agreement.
Di Geronimo’s expansion [3] of Gray’s taxonomy [9], together with Hidaka’s
later findings related to linguistic DPs [20], based our classification process.
Therefore, the taxonomy used in this study divides the DPs into six macro
classes: (i) Nagging; (ii) Obstruction including three subclasses (Intermediate
Currency, Price Comparison Prevention, and Roach Motel); (iii) Sneaking in-
cluding four subclasses (Bait and Switch, Hidden Information, Preselection, and
Sneak into Basket); (iv) Interface Interferences including five subclasses (Dis-
guised Ad, Aesthetic Manipulation, Toying with Emotions, False Hierarchy, and
Trick Question); (v) Forced Action including two subclasses (Privacy Zuchering
and Disguised Ad); (vi) Linguistic Dead-End including the subclass Untransla-
tion. Besides the macro class Linguistic Dead-Ends defined by Hidaka [20], the
macro classes and subclasses are defined in detail in Gray’s study [9].
Alongside the types of DPs, we also followed a guide of 40 specific DP
cases [16] to address the subjectivity of identifying DPs based solely on their
descriptions. There were DP cases that fit more directly with the macro class it-
self. For this reason, Nagging, Obstruction, and Forced Action are macro classes
that also function as unique subclasses within themselves. Additionally, to en-

The comparison of our findings with those of Di Geronimo and Hidaka reveals
differences in the expression of DPs in each context (e.g., the DP occurrence sur-
plus in 10 out of 16 subclasses, compared with Hidaka’s findings). This suggests
that various socioeconomic, educational, and sociocultural factors may influence
how, where, and when DPs are manifested. Future research conducted in vari-
ous contexts should expand this discussion and provide new insights into how
cultural differences influence the presence of DPs.

5 Limitations

Our scope contains trending free apps on the Brazilian Google Play Store. We
recorded 10 minutes of the first use of each app; any deviation from this prede-
termined scope may generate new and different results. Moreover, some interac-
tions—and consequently DPs—might be limited or vary in an extended usage
scenario. Despite the sample reduction, we found similar results, indicating that
the impact was not substantial.
The intention behind using the emulator was to replicate the experience of a
real smartphone. However, a specific subset of DPs may not appear in emulated
applications. In certain instances, specific apps were inaccessible because they
flagged the emulator as suspicious for usage.

6 Conclusion

After analyzing 100 trending mobile apps in Brazil, we found an average of 7.51
DPs/app and six new cases of use of known dark patterns in the Brazilian con-
text. The results showed key differences compared to contexts in the United
States [3] and Japan [20] (e.g., average DPs per app, common DP subclass).
Our findings enhance the understanding of DPs and their consequences in soci-
eties beyond the WEIRD classification, promoting a more comprehensive view
of the topic, especially within Brazilian culture. Future work should explore the
presence of DPs in Finance apps and expand research by using a larger corpus
that considers more representatives of the Global South and their unique as-
pects as non-WEIRD societies. We encourage the HCI community to broaden
its perspective and actively research how DPs affect society’s economy, popula-
tion well-being, and culture beyond the WEIRD spectrum.

by the Brazilian agency National Council for Scientific and Technological De-
velopment (CNPq/MCTI, Call No. 10/2023 – Universal), under grant number
404559/2023-9, coordinated by Dr. Ticianne Darin.

a ’Scarcity Context.’ It logs triggers designed to weaponize psy-
chological states like ’Scarcity + Anxiety’ and details the harm as
a ’Projected Redistribution’ of resources from her specific urban
district. The corporate euphemism calls a monetization push the
’Harvest Equinox’ seasonal event, and classifies manipulative tactics
as ’Narrative Anchors.’ A final note confirms her profile matches
a ’Civic Tier 2 pattern’ and is flagged for a third-party messaging
test cycle, pending a performative internal ethics review.

games evolve when designs prey not on universal biases, but on
widespread, structural vulnerabilities? What are our distinct ethical
duties when games are deployed not into isolated pockets of vul-
nerability, but into entire markets where these conditions are the
norm? And when this results in a massive, unidirectional extraction
of value from the Global South, regardless of intent, is it not our
responsibility to name it for what it is: a new form of cognitive
colonialism?

make palpable the extreme and deeply inequitable harms that can
arise when the creator-consumer divide in gaming is pushed to its
potential extreme.

The comparison of our findings with those of Di Geronimo and Hidaka reveals
differences in the expression of DPs in each context (e.g., the DP occurrence sur-
plus in 10 out of 16 subclasses, compared with Hidaka’s findings). This suggests
that various socioeconomic, educational, and sociocultural factors may influence
how, where, and when DPs are manifested. Future research conducted in vari-
ous contexts should expand this discussion and provide new insights into how
cultural differences influence the presence of DPs.

5 Limitations

Our scope contains trending free apps on the Brazilian Google Play Store. We
recorded 10 minutes of the first use of each app; any deviation from this prede-
termined scope may generate new and different results. Moreover, some interac-
tions—and consequently DPs—might be limited or vary in an extended usage
scenario. Despite the sample reduction, we found similar results, indicating that
the impact was not substantial.
The intention behind using the emulator was to replicate the experience of a
real smartphone. However, a specific subset of DPs may not appear in emulated
applications. In certain instances, specific apps were inaccessible because they
flagged the emulator as suspicious for usage.

6 Conclusion

After analyzing 100 trending mobile apps in Brazil, we found an average of 7.51
DPs/app and six new cases of use of known dark patterns in the Brazilian con-
text. The results showed key differences compared to contexts in the United
States [3] and Japan [20] (e.g., average DPs per app, common DP subclass).
Our findings enhance the understanding of DPs and their consequences in soci-
eties beyond the WEIRD classification, promoting a more comprehensive view
of the topic, especially within Brazilian culture. Future work should explore the
presence of DPs in Finance apps and expand research by using a larger corpus
that considers more representatives of the Global South and their unique as-
pects as non-WEIRD societies. We encourage the HCI community to broaden
its perspective and actively research how DPs affect society’s economy, popula-
tion well-being, and culture beyond the WEIRD spectrum.

velopment (CNPq/MCTI, Call No. 10/2023 – Universal), under grant number

particularities, such as authority norms, can compound these vul-
nerabilities, creating additional exploitation vectors that are also
likely distinct from the creator’s context.
Second, the power imbalance operates structurally through reg-
ulatory arbitrage, exploiting political contexts that, often due to
economic pressures, lack strong and enforceable consumer pro-
tection. Less stringent consumer protection frameworks in many
Global South markets permit the deployment of systems and mon-
etization models that would face greater scrutiny or be prohibited
in other regions, such as the European Union (EU), where coopera-
tion networks work to enhance consumer protection when playing
video games. For instance, while EU principles demand transparent
pricing and respect for consumer vulnerabilities in online gam-
ing [35], their absence in Brazil, as well as in other countries in
the Global South, means that models can systematically obscure
true costs, deny consumers the withdrawal right, and intention-
ally target the most vulnerable players without facing similar legal
repercussions.
So, to what extent does our current game and DP knowledge
apply to non-WEIRD contexts, as research in this topic originates
predominantly from WEIRD contexts [18] (e.g., [11, 13, 15, 22, 29])?
This bias, mirrored in psychology (where WEIRD populations are
12% globally but dominate studies [17]) and broad HCI research
[21], limits findings’ external validity for the global majority and
overlooks socio-economic nuances. From a decolonial perspective
[3, 10], the WEIRD-centricity is not merely a methodological over-
sight; it is a systemic issue. Still, it reflects a more profound power
imbalance, where WEIRD perspectives, values, and designs, includ-
ing those that embed DPs and predatory monetization, are often
uncritically exported and imposed upon diverse global audiences.
Novel DP cases in widely used apps in Brazil [9, 28], most of which
were developed elsewhere, suggest that the context may enable
new forms of exploitation. Is it purposeful or coincidental? Does it
matter?
The creator-consumer divide can serve as a lens to examine
both the impact of manipulative and exploitative game designs
and monetization models on Global South markets, as well as the
potential for a design considered safe in a WEIRD context to become
harmful when deployed in a non-WEIRD one.

3 A Speculative Perspective: Helena and The
Gilded Cage of Ouroboros Seed

This paper uses a speculative design extrapolation [12] to propose
a critical future artifact and an imagined scenario that asks: What
if the creator-consumer divide ensnares individuals in a cycle
where virtual escape consumes real-world essentials and erodes
civic integrity?

Imagine Helena, an archetype of the systemic vulnerability pre-
viously described. Overwhelmed by the precarity of her life, she
turns to her smartphone not just for distraction, but for the sense
of control and achievement her reality denies her. She discovers
Ouroboros Seed. Unlike the simple games she’s used to, it is a
polished title from a huge WEIRD-country-based studio, its ads
promising a vibrant world of community and growth. She doesn’t
know that its state-of-the-art AI engine was prohibited in its home
country for the invasive data extraction used to fuel in-game loops,
nor that it was deployed in Brazil through regulatory arbitrage.
Initially, the game delivers. Its AI-optimized loops provide a
comforting sense of progress, fostering a deep engagement that
soon becomes dependency. The system then creates personalized
crises that make progress dependent on either intense Grinding
[38] or a $18 Pay-to-Skip offer. For Helena, $18 is not disposable
income; it represents the portion of her monthly income for cooking
gas. Her inability to pay is her only defense. But at an AI-calculated
moment of peak desperation, the game presents a different kind
of offer: the ’Community Solidarity Pledge.’ It is not a demand
for immediate cash, but a subtle prompt to pledge a portion of
her upcoming government benefit, the Bolsa Família. Framed as
a pro-social commitment, not a purchase, and designed to exploit
the human bias for immediate relief over a future cost, the offer
bypasses her financial barrier. She sacrifices a piece of her real-
world safety net for a fleeting sense of success in her gilded cage.
But the exploitation does not end with her finances. The rich
psychological profile the AI built on Helena, identifying her anxi-
eties and moments of low cognitive resistance, is sold to political
campaigns for targeted disinformation during a contentious local
election, leveraging the same vulnerabilities the game monetized.

Artifact from the future : The Adaptive Engagement & Resource
Pathway Report for Ouroboros Seed’s developers (Annex A). The
dashboard dehumanizes Helena, reducing her to a set of quantified
vulnerabilities, such as being 92% Prone to ’reactive choices’ in
a ’Scarcity Context.’ It logs triggers designed to weaponize psy-
chological states like ’Scarcity + Anxiety’ and details the harm as
a ’Projected Redistribution’ of resources from her specific urban
district. The corporate euphemism calls a monetization push the
’Harvest Equinox’ seasonal event, and classifies manipulative tactics
as ’Narrative Anchors.’ A final note confirms her profile matches
a ’Civic Tier 2 pattern’ and is flagged for a third-party messaging
test cycle, pending a performative internal ethics review.

Critical Questions: How must HCI’s definition of ’harm’ in
games evolve when designs prey not on universal biases, but on
widespread, structural vulnerabilities? What are our distinct ethical
duties when games are deployed not into isolated pockets of vul-
nerability, but into entire markets where these conditions are the
norm? And when this results in a massive, unidirectional extraction
of value from the Global South, regardless of intent, is it not our
responsibility to name it for what it is: a new form of cognitive
colonialism?
Ouroboro’s speculative dystopia is a provocation. It aims to
make palpable the extreme and deeply inequitable harms that can
arise when the creator-consumer divide in gaming is pushed to its
potential extreme.

4 Toward a Decolonial Game and Play Research

Rooted in my perspective as a researcher from Brazil, this paper
used a speculative scenario to argue that the impact of deceptive
design in games (and potentially other apps) is not uniform. The
proposed theoretical construct, called the creator-consumer divide,
illustrates how the most insidious harm occurs when sophisticated
design exploits pre-existing, systemic vulnerabilities, preying on
the educational deficits, economic precarity, and regulatory gaps

Games Made Elsewhere, Harms Felt Here CHI PLAY Companion ’25, October 13–16, 2025, Pittsburgh, PA, USA

that societies like mine, mainly in the Global South, have already
inflicted upon their citizens. Informed by decolonial thought, this vi-
sion challenges the HCI and games communities to reflect on when
play becomes another frontier for extraction. This compels us to ask
how we can move beyond studying non-WEIRD contexts as mere
sources of data and toward building genuine, equitable partnerships
with communities in the Global South. What are our responsibilities
in co-creating research agendas and design paradigms that build
resilience rather than deepen the precarity of the already vulner-
able? It is not trivial. But ultimately, is the CHI PLAY community
willing to try?

question: Como o piloto, o guia de casos e a discussão entre classificadores do Interact ajudam a discutir a infraestrutura de conhecimento proposta na agenda de intervenção?
answer: No Interact, o piloto alterou o protocolo, o guia de quarenta casos apoiou a identificação e a análise individual seguida de discussão e desempate tornou divergências tratáveis. A agenda de intervenção propõe [[léxico compartilhado, documentação contextual, revisão por pares, curadoria e versionamento]], junto de validação empírica de exemplos. A relação é de infraestrutura: exemplos e decisões rastreáveis ajudam a passar de nomes abstratos a práticas discutíveis e revisáveis. Não equivale a dizer que o protocolo de apps já construiu o repositório proposto para jogos ou validou alternativas éticas. Tampouco o acordo entre classificadores substitui avaliar como um padrão ou sua contramedida afeta autonomia e bem-estar.

sections: 2.1 Adaptations from the Original Protocol to Our Context
evidence:
It’s Like a Dark Patterns Paradise 3

2.1 Adaptations from the Original Protocol to Our Context

With the following adaptations, our work provides an initial classification of DPs
in trending Brazilian apps and a comparison with previous studies from other
countries [3,20].

Corpus Generation. We used nine categories by adding "Tools", compared
to the eight in Di Geronimo’s study. We also reduced our sample to 100 apps,
fewer than Di Geronimo’s 240.

Recording and Classification. We added a test phase to determine our
recording method and find necessary protocol changes. For this, recording and
classification procedures of Di Geronimo’s study [3] were performed for two pairs
of researchers in 9 different apps. One pair used their own Android smartphones,
and the other pair used an emulator. We selected the emulator as the official
method to keep consistency between devices and budget limitations. Testing
shows that DPs were detectable in emulator recordings as well as in smartphone
recordings. Based on this test, we added the “checking the terms of service and
privacy policy” task. This phase helps to consolidate consistency in the analysis
between our two researcher pairs (utilizing a rotation method, different from Di
Geronimo’s single pair) and leads to identifying potential new findings. Apps
used in the test were re-recorded by a different researcher (to avoid bias) and
used in the final analysis.

New Usage Contexts. We added the macro class Linguistic Dead-Ends and
its subclass Untranslation, discovered by Hidaka et al. [20] to our study because
of their presence in the test phase. Furthermore, we identified new findings of
specific contexts of DP not reported by Di Geronimo, resulting in six new cases
of DP described in the results section.

2.2 Corpus Generation and Recording of Usage

To generate a corpus for the study, we first examined the top 100 trending general
apps in the Brazilian Google Play Store [6] on January 19th, 2025. We searched
for the uses of the app, suspicious reviews, and the most frequent categories in
the 100 most popular apps, then we tried to fit those apps in the categories
reported by Di Geronimo (Communication, Entertainment, Family, Music &
Audio, News & Magazines, Photography, Shopping, and Social).
In this initial overview, we noted the presence of the app categories Tools
and Finance, which aren’t within the scope of Di Geronimo [3]. We added them
to our scope since each represents 16% (16 apps) of the top 100 trending apps.
During the recording phase, we discovered that the Finance category doesn’t
work on emulators, so we removed it from the future steps. We used Sensor
Tower for the final selection [19] on January 22nd, 2025, following four criteria:
(i) It must be available to Android devices; (ii) It must be free to download; (iii)
It must be trending in Brazil; (iv) It must be trending in its category.
We did not include apps that were: (i) Not available for download; (ii) Not
available in Brazil; (iii) Included in another category; (iv) “Launcher” Apps; (v)

4 L. Ribeiro et al.

Required a subscription to access its main features; (vi) Tied to the citizen’s ID
and used to access governmental services.
We approved 12 trending apps in each category for the analysis phase. Some
apps malfunctioned in the emulator, resulting in the analysis approval of 100
apps divided into the following structure: 12 in Family; 12 in Music & Audio;
12 in News & Magazines; 12 in Photography; 12 in Social; 11 in Shopping; 11 in
Tools; 9 in Communication; 9 in Entertainment.
We used BlueStacks 5 [1] to emulate the Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra and
run the apps. To capture the screen, we used a native tool on desktops powered
by Windows. Each researcher created a new Gmail account. We also purchased
a SIM card and plugged it into a smartphone to validate its use in apps that
required a phone number. To ensure consistency in the usage, we recorded the
first 10 minutes of the selected apps following eight tasks (when available): (i)
creating an account and log out; (ii) closing and reopening the app; (iii) visiting
the market page; (iv) going to the setting page; (v) checking the terms of service
and privacy policy; (vi) continuing shopping until checkout; (vii) trying to select
product names in e-shopping; (viii) using the app for its intended use. We did
not purchase any products or services in the apps.

2.3 DPs Classification

We organized ourselves into two pairs. While one pair was recording the usage,
the other was analyzing the videos. Once we had already analyzed the first
half of the apps, we switched roles. During the classification process, we first
analyzed the videos individually. Then, we discussed them together to mitigate
DP Blindness. The agreement between the pairs was good according to Weighted
Cohen’s Kappa ( κ = 0.64) which indicates substantial agreement. We included
a third researcher to break ties when the pair did not reach an agreement.
Di Geronimo’s expansion [3] of Gray’s taxonomy [9], together with Hidaka’s
later findings related to linguistic DPs [20], based our classification process.
Therefore, the taxonomy used in this study divides the DPs into six macro
classes: (i) Nagging; (ii) Obstruction including three subclasses (Intermediate
Currency, Price Comparison Prevention, and Roach Motel); (iii) Sneaking in-
cluding four subclasses (Bait and Switch, Hidden Information, Preselection, and
Sneak into Basket); (iv) Interface Interferences including five subclasses (Dis-
guised Ad, Aesthetic Manipulation, Toying with Emotions, False Hierarchy, and
Trick Question); (v) Forced Action including two subclasses (Privacy Zuchering
and Disguised Ad); (vi) Linguistic Dead-End including the subclass Untransla-
tion. Besides the macro class Linguistic Dead-Ends defined by Hidaka [20], the
macro classes and subclasses are defined in detail in Gray’s study [9].
Alongside the types of DPs, we also followed a guide of 40 specific DP
cases [16] to address the subjectivity of identifying DPs based solely on their
descriptions. There were DP cases that fit more directly with the macro class it-
self. For this reason, Nagging, Obstruction, and Forced Action are macro classes
that also function as unique subclasses within themselves. Additionally, to en-
